            "Yes. For what you want, the cleanest candidate is probably not the nucleus at all. It is the free electron.\n\nThe reason is that you want three things simultaneously:\n\n1. a fundamental or near-fundamental object,\n2. a characteristic length scale,\n3. an intrinsic oscillation that survives in the ground/free state and is not merely an excitation mode.\n\nThe electron gives you the cleanest standard-physics pair of scales:\n\n\\[\n\\lambda_C=\\frac{h}{m_ec}\n\\]\n\nor reduced Compton wavelength\n\n\\[\n\\bar\\lambda_C=\\frac{\\hbar}{m_ec},\n\\]\n\nand the corresponding Compton angular frequency\n\n\\[\n\\omega_C=\\frac{m_ec^2}{\\hbar}.\n\\]\n\nThese are not excitation frequencies. They are set by the electron rest mass itself.\n\nThere is also the Dirac zitterbewegung frequency,\n\n\\[\n\\omega_{\\rm ZB}=\\frac{2m_ec^2}{\\hbar}=2\\omega_C,\n\\]\n\nwhich appears in the standard Dirac analysis of the free electron. Whether zitterbewegung should be interpreted as literal internal motion is a separate question; standard quantum theory does not require that interpretation. But mathematically it is exactly the kind of persistent intrinsic frequency you are asking for. There is a substantial literature connecting it to de Broglie’s “internal clock” idea. citeturn361582academia48turn361582academia49\n\nAnd now notice what happens if we temporarily forget those labels and just feed the two standard scales into the helix grammar.\n\nTake\n\n\\[\nR=\\bar\\lambda_C=\\frac{\\hbar}{mc},\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\omega=\\omega_C=\\frac{mc^2}{\\hbar}.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{R\\omega=c}.\n\\]\n\nThat is strikingly economical.\n\nThe transverse tangential speed of the corresponding circular phase motion would be exactly \\(c\\):\n\n\\[\nv_\\perp=R\\omega=c.\n\\]\n\nIf instead the relevant intrinsic frequency is the zitterbewegung frequency,\n\n\\[\n\\omega_{\\rm ZB}=2\\omega_C,\n\\]\n\nthen the radius required for the same \\(c\\) tangential speed is\n\n\\[\nR_{\\rm ZB}\n=\n\\frac{c}{\\omega_{\\rm ZB}}\n=\n\\frac{\\hbar}{2mc}\n=\n\\frac{\\bar\\lambda_C}{2}.\n\\]\n\nAgain,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{R_{\\rm ZB}\\omega_{\\rm ZB}=c}.\n\\]\n\nThat pair is worth putting a large circle around, because nothing was added:\n\n\\[\nm,\\quad c,\\quad \\hbar\n\\]\n\nalready belong to standard relativistic quantum mechanics, and they independently generate a length and a frequency whose product is \\(c\\).\n\nIn the spring grammar:\n\n\\[\n\\text{diameter}=2R\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\text{period}=\\frac{2\\pi}{\\omega}.\n\\]\n\nFor the Compton choice,\n\n\\[\nD=2\\frac{\\hbar}{mc},\n\\]\n\n\\[\nT_C=\\frac{2\\pi\\hbar}{mc^2}\n=\\frac{h}{mc^2}.\n\\]\n\nSo the circumference traversed in one period is\n\n\\[\n2\\pi R\n=\n\\frac{2\\pi\\hbar}{mc},\n\\]\n\nwhile\n\n\\[\ncT_C\n=\nc\\frac{2\\pi\\hbar}{mc^2}\n=\n\\frac{2\\pi\\hbar}{mc}.\n\\]\n\nThus\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{2\\pi R=cT_C}.\n\\]\n\nThat is literally the circumference/time relation for uniform circular motion at \\(c\\).\n\nThis is substantially cleaner than starting with \\(^3\\)He, because the electron doesn't force us first to disentangle nuclear collective dynamics, binding, constituent structure, and excitations.\n\nAnd there's another important piece. In relativistic quantum mechanics a free massive particle accumulates proper-time phase as\n\n\\[\n\\phi=\\frac{mc^2}{\\hbar}\\tau.\n\\]\n\nTherefore\n\n\\[\n\\frac{d\\phi}{d\\tau}\n=\n\\frac{mc^2}{\\hbar}\n=\n\\omega_C.\n\\]\n\nSo the Compton oscillation is not something we have to invent from an analogy with a spring. The phase of a massive relativistic quantum object already rotates at exactly that proper-time rate.\n\nNow geometrize the phase:\n\n\\[\ne^{-i\\omega_C\\tau}\n\\quad\\longleftrightarrow\\quad\n(\\cos\\omega_C\\tau,\\sin\\omega_C\\tau).\n\\]\n\nThat gives the circular part.\n\nLet the worldline simultaneously advance through Minkowski spacetime.\n\nYou now have precisely the construction we've been discussing:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{worldline advance}+\\text{intrinsic phase rotation}}\n\\]\n\nwhich geometrically becomes a helix once the phase circle is represented explicitly.\n\nThat doesn't establish that an electron physically is a little corkscrew. But as a strictly Minkowski-geometric representation of standard relativistic quantum mechanics, it is an unusually clean starting case.\n\nAnd it gets better when you ask for a minimal pair.\n\nElectron and muon are nearly ideal.\n\nStandard physics says they have:\n\n- the same electric charge,\n- the same spin \\(1/2\\),\n- the same lepton character,\n- essentially the same point-particle interaction structure,\n\nbut very different masses.\n\nSo if\n\n\\[\nR\\propto\\frac1m\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\omega\\propto m,\n\\]\n\nthen going from electron to muon should simply shrink the radius and increase the winding rate by the same mass ratio:\n\n\\[\n\\frac{R_\\mu}{R_e}\n=\n\\frac{m_e}{m_\\mu},\n\\]\n\nwhile\n\n\\[\n\\frac{\\omega_\\mu}{\\omega_e}\n=\n\\frac{m_\\mu}{m_e}.\n\\]\n\nTheir product remains\n\n\\[\nR\\omega=c.\n\\]\n\nThat's exactly the kind of minimal-pair geometry you described: almost everything held fixed, one standard-physics parameter—mass—changed, and the Minkowski spring representation tells you immediately what should change geometrically.\n\nThen tau gives a third point.\n\nSo before touching proton/neutron or \\(^3\\)He, I would probably establish the H(s)H “order-1 spring ruler” using:\n\n\\[\ne,\\quad \\mu,\\quad \\tau.\n\\]\n\nIf the same construction survives all three with no additional ingredients, then we have a very clean baseline for what mass does to a worldtube spring.\n\nAfter that, proton/neutron and \\(^3\\)He become the much more interesting braided/composite cases."

            "In SAT’s grammar: yes, we now have a very specific candidate electron geometry.\n\nNot because standard physics says “the electron is literally a helix,” but because once SAT insists that every persistent internal/external action must live on the same worldline/worldtube as deflection, oscillation, or nested oscillation, the free-electron Dirac scales give us an unusually constrained order-1 construction.\n\nThe cleanest pair is:\n\n\\[\n\\omega_C=\\frac{m_ec^2}{\\hbar}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\bar\\lambda_C=\\frac{\\hbar}{m_ec}.\n\\]\n\nFor the electron,\n\n\\[\n\\bar\\lambda_C=3.8615926744\\times10^{-13}\\ {\\rm m}.\n\\]\n\nThose are standard relativistic quantum scales. citeturn336626search24turn336626search25\n\nAnd they satisfy exactly\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\bar\\lambda_C\\,\\omega_C=c.}\n\\]\n\nSo if SAT maps the intrinsic phase oscillation onto a circular transverse component of the worldline, the obvious order-1 helix has\n\n\\[\nR=\\bar\\lambda_C,\n\\qquad\n\\omega=\\omega_C,\n\\]\n\nand therefore transverse tangential rate\n\n\\[\nR\\omega=c.\n\\]\n\nThen the diameter is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_e=2\\bar\\lambda_C\n=\n7.7231853488\\times10^{-13}\\ {\\rm m}.\n}\n\\]\n\nBut there is a second, equally natural convention coming specifically from the Dirac zitterbewegung scale:\n\n\\[\n\\omega_Z=\\frac{2m_ec^2}{\\hbar}=2\\omega_C.\n\\]\n\nThe corresponding light-speed circular radius is\n\n\\[\nR_Z=\\frac{c}{\\omega_Z}\n=\n\\frac{\\hbar}{2m_ec}\n=\n\\frac{\\bar\\lambda_C}{2}.\n\\]\n\nSo\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR_Z=1.9307963372\\times10^{-13}\\ {\\rm m}\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_Z=\\bar\\lambda_C\n=\n3.8615926744\\times10^{-13}\\ {\\rm m}.\n}\n\\]\n\nAgain,\n\n\\[\nR_Z\\omega_Z=c.\n\\]\n\nThe zitterbewegung frequency \\(2mc^2/\\hbar\\) is indeed the standard Dirac frequency scale associated with interference between positive- and negative-energy components. citeturn336626search27turn336626academia28\n\nSo I would say we know the electron’s SAT spring to within one very specific factor-of-two question:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{Is the geometrized circular period the Compton phase period or the Dirac ZB period?}\n}\n\\]\n\nThat is not a free parameter. It should be decidable from the rest of the geometry.\n\nAnd SAT gives us a nice way to phrase the distinction.\n\nIf one full turn of the internal geometric phase corresponds to\n\n\\[\n\\Delta\\phi=2\\pi,\n\\]\n\nthen\n\n\\[\n\\omega=\\omega_C\n\\]\n\nnaturally gives\n\n\\[\nR=\\bar\\lambda_C.\n\\]\n\nIf the physically relevant closed worldline oscillation is the positive/negative-frequency beating,\n\n\\[\n(+\\omega_C)-(-\\omega_C)=2\\omega_C,\n\\]\n\nthen the observed oscillatory rate is\n\n\\[\n\\omega_Z=2\\omega_C\n\\]\n\nand the corresponding radius is\n\n\\[\nR=\\frac{\\bar\\lambda_C}{2}.\n\\]\n\nThat factor of two is potentially not annoying at all, because spin-\\(\\tfrac12\\) geometry already has a \\(4\\pi\\), rather than \\(2\\pi\\), return structure. I would not equate those casually, but they belong in the same audit.\n\nSo the candidate order-1 electron worldline is\n\n\\[\nH(\\tau)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\nR\\cos(\\omega\\tau)\\\\\nR\\sin(\\omega\\tau)\\\\\n\\text{longitudinal advance}\n\\end{pmatrix},\n\\]\n\nwith\n\n\\[\nR\\omega=c.\n\\]\n\nThen all the “spring” properties become fixed functions of the longitudinal rate \\(v_\\parallel\\):\n\n\\[\nP=\\frac{2\\pi v_\\parallel}{\\omega},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\tan\\alpha\n=\n\\frac{v_\\parallel}{R\\omega}\n=\n\\frac{v_\\parallel}{c},\n\\]\n\nand therefore\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\tan\\alpha=\\beta}\n\\]\n\nfor this simplest parameterization, where\n\n\\[\n\\beta=\\frac{v_\\parallel}{c}.\n\\]\n\nThat is potentially very interesting.\n\nAt rest,\n\n\\[\nv_\\parallel=0,\n\\]\n\nso the order-1 trace collapses to pure cyclic motion in the transverse phase plane.\n\nAs the electron acquires translational velocity, the same cyclic motion is carried forward, giving a helix whose pitch increases with \\(v\\).\n\nThat immediately gives:\n\n\\[\nP\n=\n\\frac{2\\pi v}{\\omega_C}\n=\n\\beta\\,2\\pi\\bar\\lambda_C\n=\n\\boxed{\\beta\\lambda_C}\n\\]\n\nunder the Compton convention.\n\nSo the ordinary Compton wavelength appears as the pitch scale at \\(v=c\\):\n\n\\[\nP_{\\beta=1}=\\lambda_C.\n\\]\n\nThat is not something we separately inserted; it follows from\n\n\\[\nR=\\bar\\lambda_C,\\qquad R\\omega=c.\n\\]\n\nNow, there is one relativistic refinement we should make before treating that as final. The intrinsic oscillation is naturally expressed in **proper time**:\n\n\\[\n\\phi=\\omega_C\\tau.\n\\]\n\nAn external observer uses coordinate time,\n\n\\[\nd\\tau=\\frac{dt}{\\gamma},\n\\]\n\nso they see\n\n\\[\n\\omega_{\\rm observed}=\\frac{\\omega_C}{\\gamma}.\n\\]\n\nMeanwhile the longitudinal motion is\n\n\\[\nz=vt.\n\\]\n\nTherefore one cycle of internal proper-time phase corresponds in the lab frame to\n\n\\[\n\\Delta t\n=\n\\gamma\\frac{2\\pi}{\\omega_C},\n\\]\n\ngiving pitch\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(v)\n=\nv\\Delta t\n=\n\\gamma\\beta\\,\\lambda_C.\n}\n\\]\n\nThat is much better, because now the helix geometry carries ordinary relativistic time dilation automatically.\n\nSo the moving electron candidate becomes\n\n\\[\nR=\\bar\\lambda_C\n\\]\n\nin its intrinsic transverse construction,\n\nwhile\n\n\\[\nP=\\gamma\\beta\\lambda_C.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\frac{P}{2\\pi R}\n=\n\\gamma\\beta.\n\\]\n\nAnd since\n\n\\[\n\\gamma\\beta=\\frac{p}{mc},\n\\]\n\nwe get\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{P}{2\\pi R}\n=\n\\frac{p}{mc}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThat is a really useful result.\n\nThe **dimensionless tightness/slope of the spring is directly the relativistic momentum in units of \\(mc\\)**.\n\nEquivalently,\n\n\\[\nP\n=\n\\frac{h}{mc}\\frac{p}{mc}\n=\n\\frac{hp}{m^2c^2}.\n\\]\n\nI would not interpret that too quickly yet. But it means that once we take the standard Compton phase seriously and put it literally on a Minkowski worldline, the helix shape is no longer arbitrary.\n\nMass fixes the diameter.\n\nVelocity/momentum fixes the pitch.\n\nProper-time phase fixes the winding rate.\n\nAnd\n\n\\[\nR\\omega=c\n\\]\n\nfixes their relation.\n\nSo yes: for SAT, I think we now have the first really hard-edged candidate for what a free electron “looks like” in the allowed grammar:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{an order-1 Minkowski helix whose transverse scale is Compton,\nwhose intrinsic winding is Compton/ZB frequency,\nand whose pitch is set by relativistic motion.}\n}\n\\]\n\nThe next thing I would test before touching anything else is whether the resulting helix’s curvature, torsion, angular momentum, and \\(4\\pi\\) closure reproduce the standard electron invariants without adding a single quantity. That should decide the Compton-vs-half-Compton radius convention very quickly."

            "Not automatically.\n\nAn ordinary geometric helix/spring as an unframed curve has ordinary \\(2\\pi\\) rotational symmetry.             "I think “frame” and “sheath” both bias the picture toward a tube wrapped around something more fundamental. If the filament itself is an Einstein–Rosen bridge, then the transverse structure is intrinsic geometry, not an accessory.\n\nAnd that gives us a very concrete first question: does the ER geometry itself provide the radial scale we were just trying to assign from Compton/ZB arguments?\n\nFor the standard Schwarzschild Einstein–Rosen bridge, the time-symmetric spatial slice has two asymptotically flat regions joined at a minimal \\(S^2\\) throat. In Schwarzschild coordinates the throat is at\n\n\\[\nr_s=\\frac{2GM}{c^2}.\n\\]\n\nSo the bridge itself already carries a natural transverse radius set by mass. citeturn464668academia24turn464668image1\n\nThe spatial geometry on the \\(t=0\\) Schwarzschild slice is\n\n\\[\ndl^2=\n\\frac{dr^2}{1-r_s/r}\n+r^2d\\Omega^2,\n\\]\n\nwith the minimum areal radius at\n\n\\[\nr=r_s.\n\\]\n\nAn equatorial section can be embedded as the familiar Flamm paraboloid; reflecting it across the throat gives the two-sided bridge. citeturn464668academia24\n\nimage_group{\"layout\":\"carousel\",\"aspect_ratio\":\"1:1\",\"image_refs\":[\"turn464668image1\",\"turn464668image2\"]}\n\nNow compare that scale with the one we just found from the electron's intrinsic Dirac motion:\n\n\\[\nr_{\\rm ZB}=\\frac{\\hbar}{2mc}.\n\\]\n\nThese have opposite mass dependence:\n\n\\[\nr_{\\rm ER}\\propto m,\n\\qquad\nr_{\\rm ZB}\\propto \\frac1m.\n\\]\n\nFor an electron they are nowhere near one another. The ER/Schwarzschild radius is about\n\n\\[\nr_s(e)\\sim 1.35\\times10^{-57}\\ {\\rm m},\n\\]\n\nwhereas\n\n\\[\nr_{\\rm ZB}(e)\\sim1.93\\times10^{-13}\\ {\\rm m}.\n\\]\n\nThat's roughly \\(44\\) orders of magnitude apart.\n\nSo if by “Einstein–Rosen bridge” we mean the ordinary Schwarzschild bridge whose mass parameter is the electron's observed mass, then **no: it does not set the electron spring diameter we were just discussing.**\n\nBut that doesn't kill the construction. It tells us something specific about how to interrogate it.\n\nThe ER bridge has at least three geometrically distinct scales/concepts we should not conflate:\n\n\\[\n\\text{throat areal radius},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\text{proper radial distance away from the throat},\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\text{embedding width/shape of a spatial slice}.\n\\]\n\nThe familiar picture is deceptive because the embedding diagram makes the bridge look like a finite-radius tube. The actual three-dimensional spatial slice has topology\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\mathbb R\\times S^2}\n\\]\n\nwith the \\(S^2\\) attaining a minimum area at the throat. It is not literally a cylindrical pipe of constant diameter.\n\nThat is probably where your suggestion to inspect 3-D slices becomes important.\n\nInstead of asking “what is the diameter of an ER bridge?” we should look at what a **moving sequence of ER spatial sections** actually traces.\n\nA filament-worldtube built from ER throats might look more like\n\n\\[\n\\cdots\nS^2_{\\lambda-\\Delta\\lambda}\n\\rightarrow\nS^2_\\lambda\n\\rightarrow\nS^2_{\\lambda+\\Delta\\lambda}\n\\cdots\n\\]\n\nwhere the centers of those minimal two-spheres trace the filament trajectory.\n\nThen the filament has two geometries at once:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{center/throat trajectory}}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{intrinsic }S^2\\text{ cross-sectional geometry}.}\n\\]\n\nThat is much better than “centerline + sheath.”\n\nIf the throat trajectory oscillates, then the sequence of throat spheres traces the spring/worldtube. The spring radius and pitch need not equal the ER throat radius. They become higher-order geometric quantities of the trajectory of the bridge itself.\n\nSo potentially:\n\n\\[\nr_{\\rm ER}\n=\n\\text{intrinsic filament thickness},\n\\]\n\nwhile\n\n\\[\nr_{\\rm helix}\n=\n\\text{radius of the filament's oscillatory trajectory}.\n\\]\n\nThose could be radically different scales without contradiction.\n\nAnd then your earlier spring-index ratio becomes physically meaningful inside the model:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nC_{\\rm HSH}\n=\n\\frac{D_{\\rm helix}}{D_{\\rm ER}}\n}\n\\]\n\nexcept now it isn't imported from spring engineering. It is simply the ratio of the oscillation diameter to the intrinsic bridge-throat diameter.\n\nThere is another possibility worth inspecting before deciding this, though. The standard ER bridge is a very particular GR solution: Schwarzschild, vacuum, nonrotating, uncharged. The maximally extended Schwarzschild wormhole is also nontraversable; its throat does not behave like a permanent material tunnel through which signals freely pass. citeturn464668search0turn464668academia24\n\nSo if SAT/HSH means specifically “the filament is constructed out of the geometry of an ER bridge,” we need to decide how literally that imports the complete Schwarzschild solution.\n\nThere is a big difference between:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{ER topology/geometric construction}}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{a Schwarzschild ER solution with }r_s=2GM/c^2.}\n\\]\n\nThe former says two spatial sheets connect across a minimal \\(S^2\\). The latter brings along a particular metric, horizon structure, causal behavior and mass-radius relation.\n\nGiven SAT's rule, I wouldn't choose between those ahead of the calculation. We should look at the actual standard geometry and determine which pieces are forced when an ER bridge is put **on a worldline**.\n\nAnd there is a potentially beautiful point here.\n\nA conventional ER bridge is usually presented globally: two exterior spatial regions joined at a throat. But HSH wants a filament. So take the smallest local geometric unit supplied by the ER construction—the minimal \\(S^2\\)—and transport it along a timelike trajectory.\n\nThat produces a worldtube with topology roughly\n\n\\[\nS^2\\times\\mathbb R\n\\]\n\nlocally along its history.\n\nIf its trajectory undergoes cyclic transverse displacement, that whole ER-throat worldtube winds helically.\n\nThen we have three nested things without inventing any:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nS^2\\text{ throat}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{worldtube}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{helical worldtube trajectory}.\n}\n\\]\n\nAnd braiding three such worldtubes gives the next construction.\n\nSo I think your instinct is right: before assigning “electron diameter” to the helical radius, we should inspect the actual spatial geometry of the Einstein–Rosen bridge and identify every length the construction naturally supplies.\n\nSpecifically I would calculate, for a Schwarzschild ER slice:\n\n\\[\nr_{\\rm throat},\n\\]\n\nproper radial distance\n\n\\[\n\\ell(r)\n=\n\\int_{r_s}^{r}\n\\frac{dr'}{\\sqrt{1-r_s/r'}},\n\\]\n\nthe embedding profile\n\n\\[\nz(r),\n\\]\n\nthe throat's intrinsic curvature,\n\n\\[\n{}^{(2)}R=\\frac{2}{r_s^2},\n\\]\n\nand the curvature of the surrounding 3-geometry.\n\nThen we can ask which of those can plausibly correspond to the **filament diameter**, versus which belong to its longitudinal/internal structure.\n\nBecause if one of those turns out, through the same Minkowski/Dirac construction, to give\n\n\\[\n\\frac{\\hbar}{2mc}\n\\]\n\nrather than\n\n\\[\n\\frac{2Gm}{c^2},\n\\]\n\nthen we have found something genuinely nontrivial.\n\nIf none does, then the conclusion is cleaner: ER geometry supplies the filament's intrinsic microscopic throat scale, while Compton/ZB geometry supplies the larger oscillatory spring scale.\n\nAnd that would give HSH two independently inherited scales rather than two invented ones."

            "Yes — structurally, very much so.\n\nThe thing we just arrived at is not merely “Pauli exclusion rendered geometrically.” It has the extra feature that two individually reluctant/excluding structures can become *more mutually compatible in a specific complementary configuration*.\n\nThat is Cooper-pair-like.\n\nIn ordinary superconducting pairing, two fermions correlate into a special joint state—typically opposite momenta and opposite spins in the simplest \\(s\\)-wave case—\n\n\\[\n(\\mathbf k,\\uparrow),\\qquad(-\\mathbf k,\\downarrow),\n\\]\n\nso that the pair as a whole has a different symmetry than either constituent separately. Maldacena and Susskind have recently\n[L185] suggested that in a theory of dynamical gravity the entanglement of ordinary perturbative quanta\n[L186] should be viewed as creating a quantum version of an Einstein-Rosen bridge between the particles,\n[L187] or a “quantum wormhole.” We demonstrate within low-energy effective field theory that there is\n[L188] a precise sense in which electric fields can also thread such quantum wormholes. We define a non￾perturbative “wormhole susceptibility” that measures the ease of passing an electric field through\n[L189] any sort of wormhole. The susceptibility of a quantum wormhole is suppressed by powers of the\n[L190] U(1) gauge coupling relative to that for a classical wormhole but can be made numerically equal\n[L191] with a sufficiently large amount of entangled matter.\n[L192] I. INTRODUCTION\n[L193] The past decade has seen accumulating evidence of\n[L194] a deep connection between classical spacetime geome￾try and the entanglement of quantum fields. In the\n[L195] AdS/CFT context, there appears to be a precise holo￾graphic sense in which a classical geometry is “emergent”\n[L196] from quantum entanglement in a dual field theory (see\n[L197] e.g. [1–10]).\n[L198] Recently, Maldacena and Susskind have made a\n[L199] stronger statement: that the link between entangle￾ment and geometry exists even without any holographic\n[L200] changes of duality frame [11]. They propose that any en￾tangled perturbative quantum matter in the bulk of a dy￾namical theory of gravity, such as an entangled Einstein￾Podolsky-Rosen (EPR) [12] pair of electrons, is connected\n[L201] by a “quantum wormhole,” or some sort of Planckian,\n[L202] highly fluctuating, version of the classical Einstein-Rosen\n[L203] (ER) [13] bridge that connects the two sides of an eternal\n[L204] black hole. Notably, while it clearly resonates well with\n[L205] holographic ideas [14–29], this “ER = EPR” proposal\n[L206] is more general in that it makes no reference to gauge￾gravity duality. The entangled quantum fields here exist\n[L207] already in a theory of dynamical gravity rather than in\n[L208] a holographically dual field theory.\n[L209] It is not at all obvious that quantum wormholes so de￾fined – i.e. just ordinary entangled perturbative matter\n[L210] – exhibit properties similar to those of classical worm￾holes. For example, if we have dynamical electromag￾netism, then the existence of a smooth geometry in the\n[L211] throat of an Einstein-Rosen bridge means that there exist\n[L212] states with a continuously tunable1\n[L213] electric flux thread￾ing the wormhole, as shown in Figure 1."

EPR: ELEMENTS OF REALITY\n[L536] In early March 1935, Einstein, Rosen, and Podol￾sky submitted the manuscript of the EPR paper, \"Can\n[L537] Quantum-Mechanical Description of Physical Reality Be\n[L538] Considered Complete?\", to Physical Review, and it was\n[L539] published on May 15, 1935 [1]\n[L540] Einstein, Rosen, and Podolsky used the EPR thought\n[L541] experiment to demonstrate that the Heisenberg uncer￾tainty principle fails if quantum mechanics is complete.\n[L542] They first defined an \"element of reality\": If we can pre￾dict the value of a physical quantity without disturbing\n[L543] the measured system, then that quantity is an element\n[L544] of reality. In the EPR thought experiment, the state of\n[L545] particle A is dependent on the state of particle B.\n[L546] Let’s start with the momentum of particle B.\n[L547] The momentum of particle A is measured and is found\n[L548] to have a value of p. We can infer that the momentum\n[L549] of particle B is equal in magnitude but opposite in direc￾tion, −p, due to the conservation of linear momentum.\n[L550] This inference allows us to predict the value of particle\n[L551] B’s momentum without actually measuring it.\n[L552] Therefore, according to Einstein, Rosen, and Podolsky,\n[L553] the momentum of particle B is an element of reality.\n[L554] Similarly, let’s consider the position of particle B.\n[L555] We measure the position of particle A along the x￾axis and find it at position x1. According to the \"con￾servation of relative position\" (a principle invented by\n[L556] Einstein), we can conclude that particle B’s position is\n[L557] related to A’s position by a fixed separation, denoted as\n[L558] x0. Specifically, particle B’s position can be expressed as\n[L559] x2 = x1 + x0.\n[L560] Again, without directly measuring the position of par￾ticle B, we can predict its value based on the measure￾ment of particle A. Thus, the position of particle B is\n[L561] considered an element of reality.\n[L562] This suggests that particle B’s momentum and posi￾tion can be simultaneously determined, contrary to the\n[L563] uncertainty principle.\n[L564] Indeed, Einstein, Rosen, and Podolsky argued that\n[L565] these elements of reality, namely the momentum and po￾sition of particle B, contradict the Heisenberg uncertainty\n[L566] principle. The uncertainty principle states that momen￾tum and position cannot be precisely known simultane￾ously. The uncertainty principle represents the commu￾tation relationship between the operators for momentum\n[L567] P and position Q, showing that they do not commute.\n[L568] Einstein, Rosen, and Podolsky show that if quantum\n[L569] mechanics is complete, momentum and position, with\n[L570] two non-commuting operators P and Q, can have simul￾taneous reality.\n[L571] According to Einstein, Rosen, and Podolsky, since the\n[L572] two particles no longer interact at the time of measure￾ment, no real change can occur in the second particle due\n[L573] to anything that may be done to the first particle [1].\n[L574] This is the principle of local realism: particles A and B\n[L575] should only be influenced by their local interactions.\n[L576] However, when particle A’s momentum is measured,\n[L577] particle B’s momentum is inferred instantaneously with￾out disturbing particle A. This violates local realism.\n[L578] arXiv:2307.05548v2 [physics.hist-ph] 4 Sep 20232\n[L579] Einstein, Rosen, and Podolsky thus conclude: quan￾tum mechanics is incomplete."

This construction stems from the longstanding\n[L638] intuition, going back to Einstein and Rosen in 1935 [1], Schrödinger in 1956 [3], and ’t Hooft in recent\n[L639] decades [21], that a consistent quantum gravitational description of nature must involve two sheets of\n[L640] spacetime, or equivalently, two time directions connected through a quantum bridge.\n[L641] The key insight of this paper is that gravitational horizons (in black holes, de Sitter, and Rindler\n[L642] spacetimes) induce a natural partitioning of Hilbert space into geometric superselection sectors (SSS),\n[L643] each defined by discrete spacetime symmetries such as parity (P) and time reversal (T ). These sectors\n[L644] form a direct-sum structure, within which quantum fields remain globally unitary, even in spacetimes\n[L645] where standard QFT predicts loss of information or thermality.\n[L646] A unifying element in this picture is the inverted harmonic oscillator (IHO), whose quantum\n[L647] properties were reviewed in Section 3, and which recurs across all horizon-based physics as a universal\n[L648] effective degree of freedom. In Sec . 4 we showed that IHOs naturally encode the dynamics of quantum\n[L649] fields near horizons, and for a successful description of quantum fields in curved spacetime, we\n[L650] must necessarily understand our physical world with two arrows of time. In Sec. 5, we built the\n[L651] direct-sum quantum field theory that gives a new understanding of spacetime based on discrete\n[L652] transformations such as PT . This particular quantization structure with two arrows of time at the\n[L653] parity conjugate regions gives a new geometrical understanding of IHO phase space envisioned\n[L654] by Berry and Keating [22]. Our construction gives an understanding of quantum fields in curved\n[L655] spacetime with direct-sum mathematical bridges that connect the sheets of spacetime related by\n[L656] discrete space-time transformations. These mathematical bridges not only retain the vision of ER, but\n[L657] also restore the unitarity in curved spacetime. According to this framework, a pure state is a direct-sum\n[L658] (not a superposition) of two pure state components that represent the nature of the state within and\n[L659] behind the horizon (See (137), (154), (165) and also (155)). The entanglement gets spread across the\n[L660] gravitational horizon in the form of pure states dictated by discrete spacetime transformations. This\n[L661] means that an observer not only witnesses pure states evolving into pure states but also can reconstruct\n[L662] the information behind the horizon. The gravitational horizons in our construction act quantum\n[L663] mechanically as \"mirrors\" so that we not only achieve unitarity but also observer complementarity.\n[L664] This constitutes a first important step towards a consistent construction of QFTCS, which is essential\n[L665] for building quantum gravity [11,18].\n[L666] In Section 6, we reinterpreted the ER=EPR conjecture [48] through the lens of DQFT. Rather than\n[L667] requiring geometric wormholes, we argue that entangled quantum states bridging PT -conjugate\n[L668] regions realize mathematical Einstein-Rosen bridges within a single physical spacetime. This refor￾mulation not only preserves unitarity but naturally accommodates observer complementarity and\n[L669] provides a field-theoretic underpinning to quantum connectivity across horizons. Historically, the\n[L670] concept of a thermofield double state, introduced by Israel in 1976 [72], involved constructing a pure\n[L671] quantum state in an enlarged Hilbert space that is a tensor product of two copies of the original space.\n[L672] In this formalism, the second Hilbert space was considered fictitious, introduced merely to purify the\n[L673] thermal density matrix of the original system."

Introduction \n[L804] Realism is a philosophical view, according to which external reality is assumed to \n[L805] exist and have definite properties, whether or not they are observed by someone. So \n[L806] entrenched is this viewpoint in modern thinking that many scientists and philosophers \n[L807] have sought to devise conceptual foundations for quantum mechanics that are clearly \n[L808] consistent with it. One possibility, it has been hoped, is to reinterpret quantum \n[L809] mechanics in terms of a statistical account of an underlying hidden-variables theory \n[L810] in order to bring it within the general framework of classical physics. However, Bell’s \n[L811] theorem has recently shown that this cannot be done. The theorem proves that all \n[L812] realistic theories, satisfying a very simple and natural condition called locality, may be \n[L813] tested with a single experiment against quantum mechanics. These two alternatives \n[L814] necessarily lead to significantly different predictions. The theorem has thus inspired \n[L815] various experiments, most of which have yielded results in excellent agreement with \n[L816] quantum mechanics, but in disagreement with the family of local realistic theories. \n[L817] Consequently, it can now be asserted with reasonable confidence that either the thesis \n[L818] of realism or that of locality must be abandoned. Either choice will drastically change \n[L819] our concepts of reality and of space-time. \n[L820] The historical background for this result is interesting, and represents an extreme \n[L821] irony for Einstein’s steadfastly realistic position, coupled with his desire that physics \n[L822] be expressable solely in simple geometric terms. Within the realistic framework, \n[L823] Einstein et aZ(l935, hereafter referred to as EPR) presented a classic argument. As a \n[L824] starting point, they assumed the non-existence of action-at-a-distance and that some \n[L825] of the statistical predictions of quantum mechanics are correct. They considered a \n[L826] system consisting of two spatially separated but quantum-mechanically correlated \n[L827] particles. For this system, they showed that the results of various experiments are \n[L828] predetermined, but that this fact is not part of the quantum-mechanical description \n[L829] of the associated systems. Hence that description is an incomplete one. To complete \n[L830] the description, it is thus necessary to postulate additional ‘hidden variables’, which \n[L831] presumably will then restore completeness, determinism and causality to the \n[L832] theory. \n[L833] Many in the physics community rejected their argument, preferring to follow a \n[L834] counter-argument by Bohr (1935), who believed that the whole realistic viewpoint is \n[L835] inapplicable. Many others, however, felt that since both viewpoints lead to the same \n[L836] observable phenomenology, a commitment to either one is only a matter of taste. \n[L837] Hence, the discussion, for the greater part of the subsequent 30 years, was pursued \n[L838] perhaps more at physicists’ cocktail parties than in the mainstream of modern \n[L839] research. \n[L840] Starting in 1965, however, the situation changed dramatically. Using essentially \n[L841] the same postulates as those of EPR, JS Bell showed for a Gedankenexperiment of \n[L842] Bohm (a variant of that of EPR) that no deterministic local hidden-variables theory \n[L843] can reproduce all of the statistical predictions by quantum mechanics. Inspired by that \n[L844] work, Clauser et aZ(l969, hereafter referred to as CHSH) added three contributions. \n[L845] First, they showed that his analysis can be extended to cover actual systems, and that \n[L846] experimental tests of this broad class of theories can be performed.             "Got them. This is a useful set, and it separates pretty cleanly into three jobs for what we're doing.\n\nFirst, the papers that bear directly on the ER filament construction. The original Einstein–Rosen paper remains the baseline. Katanaev’s *Passing the Einstein–Rosen Bridge* keeps the two-copy Schwarzschild construction explicit: the two exterior regions are glued at \\(u=0\\), corresponding to the horizon, and investigates smooth particle trajectories through that geometry. fileciteturn1file19L75-L90 The newer Gaztañaga/Kumar/Marto work is pursuing a rather different reinterpretation—two time directions/geometric sectors and horizon oscillator structure rather than an ordinary classical wormhole—so that may be useful particularly for the timesheet/time-direction side of H(s)H, but I would not let it overwrite the original ER geometry. fileciteturn1file14L18-L39\n\nSecond—and possibly immediately important given what you just said about charge—is Engelhardt, Freivogel & Iqbal, *Electric fields and quantum wormholes*. A classical ER bridge can carry electric flux through its throat. More interestingly, they explicitly separate\n\n\\[\n\\Phi_\\Sigma=\\Phi_R+\\Phi_L\n\\]\n\nfrom\n\n\\[\n\\Phi_\\Delta=\\frac{\\Phi_R-\\Phi_L}{2}.\n\\]\n\nThe first counts net enclosed charge and is quantized in charge units; the second measures electric field threading the wormhole and can vary continuously. fileciteturn2file4L261-L300\n\nThat distinction jumps out given the geometry you've just outlined. Standard physics itself is already separating:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{net charge}}\n\\]\n\nfrom\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{extended electric flux through the bridge}}.\n\\]\n\nSo we should absolutely examine whether your tentative division between intrinsic filament/bridge geometry and extended Kelvin-vortex/timesheet response has a counterpart there. I would not map them yet, but this paper gives us something concrete to map rather than an analogy. The authors explicitly invoke Wheeler's “charge without charge”: electric field lines threading nontrivial geometry without an ordinary localized charge source in the naive sense. fileciteturn2file0L25-L46\n\nThird is the EPR/Bell constraint set: original EPR, Bell, Aspect, Clauser–Shimony, Freedman, Mermin, etc. These aren't likely to determine filament diameter, but they are an extremely hard constraint on what the finished worldtube geometry is allowed to do.\n\nBell's original result is particularly easy to state in our current language. You cannot have an underlying description in which the two outcomes are independently local functions\n\n\\[\nA(\\mathbf a,\\lambda),\\qquad B(\\mathbf b,\\lambda)\n\\]\n\nof local analyzer settings and shared prior data \\(\\lambda\\), and still reproduce all the quantum correlations. Bell explicitly identifies locality—one distant measurement result being unaffected by operations on the other system—as the crucial restriction. fileciteturn1file13L8-L27\n\nThat doesn't say a four-dimensional worldtube geometry is impossible. It tells us exactly what it must **not reduce to**: two locally self-contained particles carrying a classical instruction set away from a common source.\n\nAnd that makes ER/EPR potentially relevant to our block-construction method for a very specific reason. If an entangled pair is represented as one globally constrained 4D geometrical object rather than two independent worldtubes plus hidden instructions, then Bell's factorization assumption is simply not the geometry being proposed. Whether that geometry reproduces the correlations is another calculation entirely—but at least we know where the tripwire is.\n\nThe historical ER/EPR papers you included are also useful here. Krizek emphasizes that Einstein's actual 1935 program was broader than the modern slogan: he hoped the many-bridge problem might eventually produce particle mass regularities and quantum restrictions from the bridge theory itself. fileciteturn2file2L131-L149 At the same time, that paper argues that the modern idea of using ER bridges specifically to explain EPR nonlocality should not simply be attributed back to Einstein. fileciteturn2file10L601-L625 That's a useful historical separation.\n\nSo for our immediate foundational work, I'd prioritize the uploaded material in this order:\n\n1. **ER/Kerr/bridge geometry** → determine what the filament actually is and what transverse dimensions it inherits.\n2. **Electric fields through ER bridges** → interrogate charge versus flux versus geometric distortion.\n3. **EPR/Bell experiments** → constrain how multiple worldtubes can be globally related.\n4. **Modern ER=EPR constructions** → inspect afterward for geometric mechanisms we've independently arrived at, rather than borrowing their theoretical machinery.\n\nI also see that several of the Bell/Aspect/Fry files are duplicates, so we only need to treat each unique paper once.\n\nThe electric-flux paper is the one I'd open up next in detail. It seems unexpectedly close to the exact charge/bridge distinction you were just trying to resolve."

EPR: ELEMENTS OF REALITY\n[L221] In early March 1935, Einstein, Rosen, and Podol￾sky submitted the manuscript of the EPR paper, \"Can\n[L222] Quantum-Mechanical Description of Physical Reality Be\n[L223] Considered Complete?\", to Physical Review, and it was\n[L224] published on May 15, 1935 [1]\n[L225] Einstein, Rosen, and Podolsky used the EPR thought\n[L226] experiment to demonstrate that the Heisenberg uncer￾tainty principle fails if quantum mechanics is complete.\n[L227] They first defined an \"element of reality\": If we can pre￾dict the value of a physical quantity without disturbing\n[L228] the measured system, then that quantity is an element\n[L229] of reality. In the EPR thought experiment, the state of\n[L230] particle A is dependent on the state of particle B.\n[L231] Let’s start with the momentum of particle B.\n[L232] The momentum of particle A is measured and is found\n[L233] to have a value of p. We can infer that the momentum\n[L234] of particle B is equal in magnitude but opposite in direc￾tion, −p, due to the conservation of linear momentum.\n[L235] This inference allows us to predict the value of particle\n[L236] B’s momentum without actually measuring it.\n[L237] Therefore, according to Einstein, Rosen, and Podolsky,\n[L238] the momentum of particle B is an element of reality.\n[L239] Similarly, let’s consider the position of particle B.\n[L240] We measure the position of particle A along the x￾axis and find it at position x1. According to the \"con￾servation of relative position\" (a principle invented by\n[L241] Einstein), we can conclude that particle B’s position is\n[L242] related to A’s position by a fixed separation, denoted as\n[L243] x0. Specifically, particle B’s position can be expressed as\n[L244] x2 = x1 + x0.\n[L245] Again, without directly measuring the position of par￾ticle B, we can predict its value based on the measure￾ment of particle A. Thus, the position of particle B is\n[L246] considered an element of reality.\n[L247] This suggests that particle B’s momentum and posi￾tion can be simultaneously determined, contrary to the\n[L248] uncertainty principle.\n[L249] Indeed, Einstein, Rosen, and Podolsky argued that\n[L250] these elements of reality, namely the momentum and po￾sition of particle B, contradict the Heisenberg uncertainty\n[L251] principle. The uncertainty principle states that momen￾tum and position cannot be precisely known simultane￾ously. The uncertainty principle represents the commu￾tation relationship between the operators for momentum\n[L252] P and position Q, showing that they do not commute.\n[L253] Einstein, Rosen, and Podolsky show that if quantum\n[L254] mechanics is complete, momentum and position, with\n[L255] two non-commuting operators P and Q, can have simul￾taneous reality.\n[L256] According to Einstein, Rosen, and Podolsky, since the\n[L257] two particles no longer interact at the time of measure￾ment, no real change can occur in the second particle due\n[L258] to anything that may be done to the first particle [1].\n[L259] This is the principle of local realism: particles A and B\n[L260] should only be influenced by their local interactions.\n[L261] However, when particle A’s momentum is measured,\n[L262] particle B’s momentum is inferred instantaneously with￾out disturbing particle A. This violates local realism.\n[L263] arXiv:2307.05548v2 [physics.hist-ph] 4 Sep 20232\n[L264] Einstein, Rosen, and Podolsky thus conclude: quan￾tum mechanics is incomplete."

            "Yes. If we strip everything else away, I think **the Core** should mean one very specific thing:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{the irreducible transverse geometry of the filament before it coils, braids, vibrates, or intersects a timesheet.}}\n\\]\n\nOn the papers we have, the cleanest candidate is the **minimal ER bridge section**.\n\nFor the ordinary Schwarzschild ER construction, the two exterior regions meet at the bifurcation sphere\n\n\\[\nr=r_h,\n\\]\n\nwhich in Einstein and Rosen's notation is \\(r=2m\\). Modern treatments likewise describe the \\(t=0\\) bridge as joining at that bifurcation \\(S^2\\). fileciteturn3file0L47-L58 fileciteturn3file1L90-L112\n\nAnd \\(r\\) here is an **areal radius**:\n\n\\[\nA_{\\rm core}=4\\pi r_h^2.\n\\]\n\nSo there is no ambiguity about what geometrical quantity the GR solution supplies. If we take a 3D slice through the filament, the primitive ER core is not a line and not really a cylindrical tube. It is a minimum-area spherical section connecting two continuations of the geometry.\n\nThere is an even better way to see its shape. On the time-symmetric Schwarzschild slice,\n\n\\[\nd\\ell^2=\n\\frac{dr^2}{1-r_h/r}+r^2d\\Omega^2.\n\\]\n\nLet \\(\\ell\\) be proper distance measured away from the throat. Near \\(r=r_h\\),\n\n\\[\nr(\\ell)\n=\nr_h+\\frac{\\ell^2}{4r_h}+O(\\ell^4).\n\\]\n\nSo locally it looks like\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{minimum }S^2\\ \\longrightarrow\\ \\text{quadratic opening on either side}.}\n\\]\n\nThat's much more precise than “tube thickness.” The core has a minimum cross-section and immediately flares away from it.\n\nFor H(s)H, in the temporary block construction, I would therefore picture the filament not as\n\n\\[\n\\text{centerline}+\\text{sheath},\n\\]\n\nbut as a continuous 4D structure whose local transverse sections contain this minimum bridge geometry. Coiling then deforms/organizes the **whole thing**. There is no separate object tracing a path.\n\nNow, importantly, the charge papers tell us **not to identify the core scale with charge yet**. A classical ER bridge can have electric flux threaded through its throat, and Engelhardt et al. distinguish net charge,\n\n\\[\n\\Phi_\\Sigma,\n\\]\n\nfrom continuously adjustable field-through-the-bridge flux,\n\n\\[\n\\Phi_\\Delta.\n\\]\n\nThose are different quantities on the same bridge geometry. fileciteturn3file1L127-L149\n\nThat fits our present discipline nicely:\n\n\\[\n\\text{Core geometry}\n\\]\n\nfirst;\n\nthen separately\n\n\\[\n\\text{what charge does to / through that geometry}.\n\\]\n\nThe original ER charged construction muddies the scale issue rather than settling it. Einstein and Rosen produced a separate charged, massless bridge solution, while treating charge and mass as independent constants; that's part of why they eventually regarded electron/proton as a multi-bridge problem. So I would not use that historical charged radius as *the* filament diameter without further reason. fileciteturn3file2L191-L203\n\nThe major unresolved piece is **rotation**.\n\nIf the actual particle filament is ER-like but spinning, then Schwarzschild's spherical minimum is probably only the zeroth-order case. We need to look at Kerr and especially Kerr–Newman spatial sections and ask:\n\n\\[\nS^2\\quad\\longrightarrow\\quad ?\n\\]\n\nunder angular momentum and charge.\n\nSpecifically we need to extract:\n\n\\[\n\\text{minimum transverse extent},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\text{major/minor radii if toroidal},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\text{ring parameter }a,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\text{horizon/ergosurface dimensions},\n\\]\n\nand whether there is **any genuine finite excluded core**.\n\nThat last point matters for the Pauli idea. The standard Kerr *ring singularity itself* is a geometrical ring locus, not automatically a finite solid core. So if H(s)H needs an absolute nonintersection thickness, we cannot quietly equate “Kerr ring radius” with “hard filament diameter.” We need the 3D Kerr/ER geometry to tell us what region, if any, is actually irreducible.\n\nSo at this stage I would write the foundational decomposition as:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\underbrace{\\text{ER/Kerr minimum geometry}}_{\\text{CORE}}\n\\;\\rightarrow\\;\n\\underbrace{\\text{persistent winding}}_{\\text{COIL}}\n\\;\\rightarrow\\;\n\\underbrace{\\text{multiple wound cores}}_{\\text{BRAID}}\n}\n\\]\n\nwith timesheet distortion, Kelvin structure, charge, mass, etc. deliberately held out of the first box until we know what the bare core is.\n\nAnd the current papers give us a solid Schwarzschild starting point:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{Core}_{J=Q=0}\n=\n\\text{minimal }S^2,\\qquad\nA=4\\pi r_h^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe Kerr papers should tell us what that becomes when \\(J\\neq0\\). That is the next thing I would want before assigning a numerical filament diameter."

            "[L2] 156 Kerr bound\n[L3] Black hole candidates and the Kerr bound\n[L4] Tomohiro Harada1(a) and Rohta Takahashi(b)\n[L5] (a)Department of Physics, Rikkyo University, Toshima, Tokyo 175-8501, Japan\n[L6] (b)Cosmic Radiation Laboratory, the Institute of Physical and Chemical Research, 2-1 Hirosawa, Wako,\n[L7] Saitama 351-0198, Japan\n[L8] Abstract\n[L9] The specific angular momentum of a Kerr black hole must not be larger than its mass\n[L10] in the geometrical units. The observational confirmation of this bound which we call\n[L11] a Kerr bound directly suggests the existence of a black hole. On the other hand, the\n[L12] violation of this bound may suggest the existence of a superspinning object which\n[L13] might be suggested from a string theory argument. In order to investigate obser￾vational testability of this bound by using the X-ray energy spectrum of black hole\n[L14] candidates, we calculate the energy spectra from an optically thick and geometrically\n[L15] thin accretion disk of a superspinning object which is described by a Kerr metric\n[L16] but whose specific angular momentum is larger than its mass, and then compare the\n[L17] spectra of this object with those of a black hole. Based on this calculation, we present\n[L18] that the observational confirmation of the Kerr bound is very hard but the violation\n[L19] of it may be detectable if only the continuum X-ray spectrum of the disk is available.\n[L20] 1 Introduction\n[L21] Black hole candidates will be directly observed by radio interferometers by X-ray satellites and gravita￾tional wave detectors in the near future. Although these candidates are most likely to be black holes, it\n[L22] is not obvious to confirm that. In principle, to prove that black hole candidates are really black holes, we\n[L23] have to show that the observed data cannot be explained by anything else. In this relation, there is an\n[L24] argument that if we can show that a sufficiently large amount of mass, say, above the model-independent\n[L25] maximum mass of neutron stars ∼ 3M\f, is compactified within the size comparable with its gravitational\n[L26] radius, general relativity assures that it is a black hole. It turns out however that this argument crucially\n[L27] depends on the cosmic censorship hypothesis [1, 2]. The singularity theorems predict the existence of\n[L28] spacetime singularities in generic spacetimes, where the spacetime curvature is singular in typical cases.\n[L29] The cosmic censorship hypothesis is an unproven hypothesis about the properties of spacetimes which are\n[L30] solutions to the Einstein equation with physically reasonable matter fields and with generic initial data.\n[L31] It claims that spacetime singularities formed in physical gravitational collapse are covered by horizons\n[L32] and hidden from any or distant observers. Thus, the cosmic censorship hypothesis ensures the future pre￾dictability of the classical theory including general relativity. On the other hand, since quantum gravity\n[L33] should replace classical general relativity in the Planckian regime, singular spacetimes in classical theory\n[L34] might be modified to regular ones in some sense. If this is true, the cosmic censorship hypothesis for the\n[L35] classical theory should be reconsidered in the new context. One of the interesting possibilities is that\n[L36] naked-singular solutions of the classical Einstein equation are physically significant in the low-curvature\n[L37] region but largely modified to be smooth spacetimes around singularities in the classical solutions due\n[L38] to quantum gravity effects. This article is based on Takahashi and Harada [3]. We use the geometrical\n[L39] units, where c = G = 1.\n[L40] The Kerr metric is a solution to the vacuum Einstein equation. This solution is stationary, axisym￾metric and asymptotically flat. Rodriguez,3,4,5,‡ and Oscar Varela 3,4,5,§\n1\n[L6] Department of Physics and Astronomy and Department of Mathematics,\n[L7] University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19104, USA 2\n[L8] Center for Applied Mathematics and Theoretical Physics,\n[L9] University of Maribor, Maribor, SI2000, Slovenia 3\n[L10] Instituto de Física Teórica UAM-CSIC, Madrid, 28049, Spain 4\n[L11] Black Hole Initiative, Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02138, USA 5\n[L12] Department of Physics, Utah State University, Logan, Utah 84322, USA\n[L13] (Received 9 August 2024; accepted 2 June 2025; published 2 July 2025)\n[L14] We derive the explicit embedding of the effective Kerr spacetimes, which are pertinent to the vanishing\n[L15] of static Love numbers, soft hair descriptions of Kerr black holes, and low-frequency scalar-Kerr scattering\n[L16] amplitudes, as solutions within N ¼ 2 supergravity. These spacetimes exhibit a hidden SLð2; RÞ × Uð1Þ or\n[L17] SOð4; 2Þ symmetry resembling the so called subtracted geometries with SLð2; RÞ × SLð2; RÞ symmetry,\n[L18] which accurately represent the near-horizon geometry of Kerr black holes and, as we will argue most\n[L19] accurately represents the internal structure of the Kerr black hole. To quantify the differences among the\n[L20] effective Kerr spacetimes, we compare their physical quantities, internal structures, and geodesic equations.\n[L21] Although their thermodynamic properties, including entropy, match those of Kerr, our study uncovers\n[L22] significant differences in the interiors of these effective Kerr solutions. A careful examination of the internal\n[L23] structure of the spacetimes highlights the distinctions between various effective Kerr geometries and their\n[L24] quasinormal spectra.\n[L25] DOI: 10.1103/zp85-xym1\n[L26] I. INTRODUCTION\n[L27] Exploring low-frequency physics within black hole\n[L28] backgrounds has proven highly fruitful for the soft hair\n[L29] of Kerr black holes descriptions, low-frequency scalar-Kerr\n[L30] scattering amplitudes and vanishing of the gravitational\n[L31] static Love numbers for rotating black holes. The guiding\n[L32] principle in this approach has been the observation that for\n[L33] certain low frequency regimes, ω ≪ 1=M, with M the\n[L34] black hole mass, one can explicitly realize a hidden\n[L35] SLð2; RÞ × SLð2; RÞ symmetry in the massless Klein￾Gordon (KG) wave equation for a propagating field.\n[L36] This symmetry does not manifest itself as an isometry of\n[L37] the background metric.\n[L38] One of the significant effective metrics associated with\n[L39] Kerr black holes is the so-called subtracted geometry [1].\n[L40] This is specifically connected to the hidden symmetries of\n[L41] Kerr black hole spacetimes via Teukolsky’s equation in the\n[L42] theory of gravitational perturbations as employed in [2].\n[L43] The key feature is that these geometries provide an\n[L44] approximation in the near-horizon region of a Kerr black\n[L45] hole, maintaining its thermodynamic properties at the outer\n[L46] event horizon and its internal structure.\n[L47] An additional collection of fundamental geometries per￾tinent to black holes are the effective near-zone metrics that\n[L48] play a crucial role in describing gravitational tidal deforma￾tions, or Love symmetries [3–5]. These different geometries\n[L49] arise from the ambiguity in how one defines the effective\n[L50] Kerr near zone expansion associated with a freedom to move\n[L51] frequency dependent terms in the Klein-Gordon (KG)\n[L52] equation. For each choice of near zone split, the leading\n[L53] order massless wave equation enjoys a generalized local\n[L54] hidden symmetry [6]. Two instances of Kerr effective\n[L55] geometry (KEG) approximations have been recently pro￾posed. On the one hand, there is a geometry preserving an\n[L56] SOð4; 2Þ found in [7] and, on the other hand, an effective\n[L57] geometry preserving an SLð2; RÞ × Uð1Þ as shown in [8].\n[L58] These are more mysterious than the SLð2; RÞ × SLð2; RÞ;\n[L59] even-though these alternative KEGs preserve the same\n[L60] thermodynamic properties of Kerr, they also realize distinct\n[L61] hidden symmetries of the KG wave equation which could\n[L62] explain the vanishing of the static Love numbers for Kerr\n[L63] black holes.             "At the moment, the cross-section is partly constrained but not yet uniquely fixed.\n\nWhat we have with some confidence is this:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{filament core} \\neq \\text{coil diameter}}\n\\]\n\nThe coil comes later from persistent oscillation. The core has to come from the intrinsic ER/Kerr geometry itself.\n\nFor the nonrotating limit, Einstein–Rosen gives us a minimum spherical throat. In the Schwarzschild case the bridge joins at the minimum \\(S^2\\) surface, so the simplest transverse section is spherical in that limit.\n\nRotation changes that picture qualitatively. Kerr replaces the Schwarzschild central structure with a ring singularity at\n\n\\[\nr=0,\\qquad \\theta=\\frac{\\pi}{2},\n\\]\n\nand introduces the rotational length\n\n\\[\na=\\frac{J}{Mc}.\n\\]\n\nThe uploaded Kerr material makes clear that the ring is literally an \\(S^1\\) locus in the equatorial plane, not a finite solid tube. fileciteturn5file8L540-L557 So \\(a\\) gives us the ring radius, but by itself it does **not** give us a finite filament thickness.\n\nAround that ring we then have finite geometric surfaces: inner horizon, outer horizon, ergosurface, etc. The outer horizon is at\n\n\\[\nr_+=M+\\sqrt{M^2-a^2}\n\\]\n\nfor neutral Kerr. fileciteturn5file5L323-L337\n\nBut that \\(r_+\\) is a Boyer–Lindquist coordinate, not a literal Euclidean radius. The cleaner invariant measure is the horizon area,\n\n\\[\nA_H=16\\pi M_{\\rm irr}^2,\n\\]\n\nwhich gives an equivalent areal radius\n\n\\[\nR_A=2M_{\\rm irr}.\n\\]\n\nThat is a legitimate finite transverse scale. fileciteturn5file7L451-L459\n\nSo right now the core looks schematically like:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{ring seed }(a)\n\\subset\n\\text{finite Kerr throat/horizon geometry}\n\\subset\n\\text{ergospheric distortion}\n}\n\\]\n\nrather than simply a round wire.\n\nAnd for an electron specifically, the really interesting constraint is that\n\n\\[\na=\\frac{J}{Mc}\n\\]\n\nwith\n\n\\[\nJ=\\frac{\\hbar}{2}\n\\]\n\ngives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\na_e=\\frac{\\hbar}{2m_ec}.\n}\n\\]\n\nCarter explicitly noted that the Kerr \\(a\\)-scale for electron-like parameters lies around the Compton scale and that Kerr–Newman has the Dirac electron gyromagnetic ratio. fileciteturn5file6L356-L375\n\nBut that still tells us the **ring radius**, not the thickness of the finite excluded core.\n\nSo the unresolved geometric question is now very precise:\n\n> On a suitable 3D spatial slice through Kerr/Kerr–Newman, what finite region naturally surrounds the ring, and what are its equatorial and polar dimensions?\n\nThat is what we need to calculate next.\n\nMy current best sketch would be something like this in transverse section:\n\n```text\n               polar direction\n                    │\n              _____ │ _____\n           .-'      │      '-.\n         .'         │         '.\n        /      finite Kerr       \\\n       |      horizon/throat      |\n       |                           |\n       |      ○─────────○          | ← ring locus / a-scale\n        \\                         /\n         '.                     .'\n           '-._______________.-'\n                    │\n                 equator\n```\n\nBut even that drawing is too spherical for rapidly rotating Kerr. The actual section should become increasingly oblate as \\(a/M\\) increases, while the ring sits in the equatorial plane.\n\nSo in terms of the quantities we eventually want for H(s)H, we currently have:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{R_{\\rm ring}=a}\n\\]\n\nknown from \\(J/M\\);\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{A_{\\rm core}\\ \\text{or}\\ R_A}\n\\]\n\navailable from horizon geometry;\n\nbut\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{d_{\\rm polar}},\\qquad\n\\boxed{d_{\\rm equatorial}}\n\\]\n\nstill need to be worked out from the intrinsic horizon/throat metric rather than guessed.\n\nOnce we have those, we can finally ask whether the cross-section is approximately circular, oblate, toroidal/ring-centered, or something more subtle—and only then compare that intrinsic core size to the electron coil radius.\n\nThat is where we are."

            "Yes. There is quite a lot we can leverage, but we should separate quantities that genuinely constrain the intrinsic cross-section from ones that constrain the later coil.\n\nThe first major point is that for an electron, the classical Kerr/Kerr–Newman black-hole horizon is not available as a literal core boundary. With electron parameters,\n\n\\[\na=\\frac{J}{mc}\\approx \\frac{\\hbar}{2m_ec}\\sim 1.93\\times 10^{-13}\\ {\\rm m},\n\\]\n\nwhile its gravitational mass length\n\n\\[\nM_g=\\frac{Gm_e}{c^2}\n\\]\n\nis about \\(10^{-57}\\) m. So the electron is fantastically over-extreme in classical Kerr–Newman terms: \\(a\\gg M_g\\), and the usual horizon condition fails. Carter was already working in essentially this parameter regime when he noted that the Kerr \\(a\\)-scale for electron-like parameters is around the Compton scale. fileciteturn5file6L356-L375\n\nThat means the quantities worth mining are not “electron horizon radius,” but observables that constrain the geometry around the Kerr ring.\n\nThe strongest empirical handles are probably these:\n\n- **Mass \\(m\\)** and **spin \\(J=\\hbar/2\\)** give \\(a=J/(mc)\\) exactly within the proposed Kerr mapping. This fixes the ring/rotational scale, not thickness.\n- **Magnetic moment and \\(g\\)-factor** constrain how charge is distributed relative to that rotation. CODATA gives\n  \\[\n  g_e=-2.00231930436092(36),\n  \\]\n  versus the ideal Kerr–Newman/Dirac value \\(g=2\\). The fractional anomaly is\n  \\[\n  a_e=1.15965218046(18)\\times10^{-3}.\n  \\]\n  citeturn937958search44turn937958search2\n- **Electric dipole moment limits** constrain any persistent fore–aft or parity-breaking distortion of the electron cross-section. That could be especially useful for deciding whether an admissible core is axisymmetric, slightly displaced, or intrinsically chiral.\n- **High-energy scattering limits on electron spatial structure** are a brutal constraint. LEP analyses have put effective electron-size limits at roughly\n  \\[\n  r_e \\lesssim 10^{-19}\\ {\\rm m}\n  \\]\n  in contact-interaction interpretations; one combined LEP analysis quotes \\(1.1\\times10^{-19}\\) m. citeturn586091search50\n\nThat last number is important because it is about six orders of magnitude smaller than\n\n\\[\na_e\\sim 10^{-13}\\ {\\rm m}.\n\\]\n\nSo if \\(a\\) is part of the H(s)H electron geometry, it cannot simply behave experimentally like an ordinary rigid charged body of radius \\(a\\). The geometry has to explain why scattering sees the electron as pointlike down to \\(\\sim10^{-19}\\) m while the intrinsic rotational/phase scale is \\(\\sim10^{-13}\\) m.\n\nThat distinction may actually help us separate **core** from **coil**:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{ordinary scattering size}\\lesssim10^{-19}\\ {\\rm m}}\n\\]\n\nversus\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{Kerr/ZB rotational scale}\\sim10^{-13}\\ {\\rm m}}.\n\\]\n\nThat is exactly the kind of six-order-of-magnitude separation one would expect if the latter is winding amplitude or 4D structure rather than literal material thickness.\n\nFor composite particles we have much richer direct spatial information. CODATA 2022 gives the proton rms charge radius\n\n\\[\nr_p=0.84075(64)\\ {\\rm fm},\n\\]\n\nand also extremely precise proton mass and magnetic moment data. citeturn586091search49turn937958search6 The neutron gives a measured mean-square charge radius\n\n\\[\n\\langle r_n^2\\rangle=-0.1155(17)\\ {\\rm fm^2},\n\\]\n\nwhich tells us about the signed radial charge structure even though the net charge is zero. citeturn586091search48\n\nThose are excellent for the later braid construction because we can compare:\n\n\\[\n\\text{mass},\\quad\nJ,\\quad\n\\mu,\\quad\nr_{\\rm charge},\\quad\nG_E(Q^2),\\quad\nG_M(Q^2).\n\\]\n\nThe full electromagnetic form factors are much more valuable than a single radius. If we construct a candidate cross-section/braid and calculate its form factor, the data tell us whether the geometry is remotely viable across momentum transfer rather than merely at \\(Q^2\\to0\\).\n\nFor nuclei, the same thing gets even better: \\(^3\\)He and tritium form factors, charge radii, magnetic moments, spin, binding energies, etc. There are public electron-scattering datasets going back decades; \\(^3\\)He charge form factors have been measured over substantial momentum-transfer ranges. citeturn586091search6\n\nSo I think the empirical attack on the core should proceed in this order:\n\n1. **Electron:** use \\(m,J,\\mu,g\\), EDM limits, and pointlike-scattering limits. This tells us how large an intrinsic Kerr-like structure may be without acting like an ordinary extended charged object.\n2. **Muon:** repeat the same construction. Because \\(a\\propto1/m\\), the rotational scale changes by the known mass ratio while charge and spin remain the same. CODATA gives the reduced muon Compton wavelength \\(1.867594306(42)\\times10^{-15}\\) m. citeturn937958search1 This is an unusually clean minimal-pair test.\n3. **Proton/neutron:** use measured form factors and radii to constrain the first composite/braided cross-section.\n4. **\\(^3\\)He/tritium:** constrain the next nesting level.\n\nFor the actual finite filament thickness, though, the electron scattering limit may currently be our most useful direct empirical ceiling:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{d_{\\rm core}\\ll a_e}\n\\]\n\nand plausibly\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{d_{\\rm core}\\lesssim 10^{-19}\\ {\\rm m}}\n\\]\n\nif the core couples to scattering in anything like an ordinary spatially extended electron.\n\nThat is not yet an equality. It is a constraint.\n\nThe other route is theoretical rather than empirical: look for a regularized Kerr/ER geometry that supplies a finite thickness around the ring. Then the experiment tells us whether that proposed thickness survives.\n\nIf you want to dig data, the most valuable public archive haul would be raw or tabulated **electron/muon scattering limits, proton \\(G_E/G_M\\), neutron \\(G_E/G_M\\), and \\(^3\\)He/tritium elastic form factors**. CODATA/PDG can anchor the scalar constants; the scattering databases give us the shape information."

            "For the **core-cross-section problem**, I want data that tell us how far we can depart from an exactly pointlike electron or muon before high-\\(Q^2\\) scattering notices. I’d rather fit the data ourselves than inherit somebody else’s “electron radius,” because those published radius limits are model-dependent.\n\nThe main place to mine is **HEPData**. CERN Open Data is much less useful for this particular job; HEPData has the numerical LEP tables already unfolded into cross sections.\n\nWhat I want first, in priority order:\n\n1. **LEP2 large-angle Bhabha scattering, \\(e^+e^-\\to e^+e^-\\).** This is the single most useful dataset for the electron core. Search HEPData for:\n   - `\"non-radiative E+ E- --> E+ E-\" 189 207 GeV`\n   - `\"Bhabha\" LEP2 differential cross section`\n   - DELPHI, OPAL, L3, ALEPH separately.\n\n   DELPHI has differential tables at 189, 192, 196, 200, 202, 205 and 207 GeV. citeturn440094search2 OPAL likewise has high-energy electron-pair angular distributions and uses the same data for contact-interaction limits. citeturn440094search7\n\n   **Download the actual tables**, preferably YAML or CSV, including:\n   \\[\n   \\sqrt s,\\quad \\cos\\theta\\ {\\rm bins},\\quad\n   \\frac{d\\sigma}{d\\cos\\theta},\n   \\]\n   statistical errors, systematic errors, and any covariance/correlation matrices. If the SM prediction is included as a separate column/table, grab that too.\n\n2. **The matching muon and tau channels from the same experiments and energies:**\n   \\[\n   e^+e^-\\to\\mu^+\\mu^-,\n   \\qquad\n   e^+e^-\\to\\tau^+\\tau^-.\n   \\]\n   This is important because electron–muon–tau are our clean minimal-pair/triple system: same charge and spin, vastly different mass. DELPHI has non-radiative \\(\\mu^+\\mu^-\\) differential distributions from 183 through 207 GeV. citeturn440094search1 OPAL has corresponding electron, muon and tau angular distributions in the same submission. citeturn440094search6\n\n   If we can compare all three with the same detector/analysis conventions, that's ideal.\n\n3. **L3 high-\\(Q^2\\) Bhabha / running-\\(\\alpha\\) data.** Search:\n   - `\"Measurement of the Running of the Electromagnetic Coupling at Large Momentum-Transfer at LEP\"`\n   - L3, 189–209 GeV.\n\n   They used about 40,000 Bhabha events and covered\n   \\[\n   1800<-Q^2<21600\\ {\\rm GeV}^2,\n   \\]\n   so this gives us an especially clean lever arm in momentum transfer. citeturn320573search9 If HEPData has the \\(Q^2\\)-binned differential tables, grab everything.\n\n4. From **CERN Document Server**, grab this specific paper if you don't already have it:\n   **D. Bourilkov, “Search for TeV Strings and New Phenomena in Bhabha Scattering at CERN LEP2,” Phys. Rev. D 62, 076005 (2000), hep-ph/0002172.**\n   \n   It combined ALEPH/L3/OPAL Bhabha data and explicitly fitted a fermion form factor\n   \\[\n   F(Q^2)=1+\\frac16Q^2r^2\n   \\]\n   to obtain\n   \\[\n   r_e<2.8\\times10^{-19}\\ {\\rm m}\n   \\]\n   at 95% CL. citeturn320573search43turn320573search0 I want this mostly as a **calibration check**: if our independent fit to the raw LEP data reproduces their scale, we know our machinery is sane.\n\nWhat I **do not** especially need yet are generic compositeness searches, excited-electron mass limits, or exotic-model bounds unless they contain useful raw angular distributions. Those turn the data into somebody else's model too early.\n\nThe key mathematical object we're trying to recover from these tables is something like\n\n\\[\nF(Q^2)\n=\n1+\\frac16\\langle r^2\\rangle Q^2\n+c_4Q^4+\\cdots,\n\\]\n\nwithout assuming at first that \\(F\\) describes a literal spherical charge ball. The \\(Q^2\\) dependence gives us a transverse scale; the angular dependence may eventually tell us whether an anisotropic/ring-like cross-section is allowed.\n\nSo if you're sitting in HEPData now, the **best first haul** would be:\n\n**DELPHI + OPAL LEP2 \\(e,e;\\mu,\\mu;\\tau,\\tau\\) differential angular distributions, with all errors and correlations.**\n\nIf it's convenient, just download the complete HEPData submission archives rather than picking tables individually. Give me those ZIP/YAML files and I can sort out what we actually need.\n\nAfter that, I’ll point you toward the proton/neutron/\\(^3\\)He form-factor archives—but those are a second stage."

            "Yes — you’re in the right general ecosystem, but **HepMC is not the database I meant**. HepMC is an event-record format/library used to represent Monte Carlo particle events. Useful later, but not where I’d start for this cross-section question.\n\nFrom the CERN Open Data page you have open, I’d pivot specifically into **DELPHI**, because CERN has now released both actual LEP collision data and matching simulation samples there. That is better than I initially implied: we may be able to work much closer to event level rather than relying only on published summary tables.\n\nFor example, CERN Open Data has real DELPHI collision datasets from LEP2 at 181–210 GeV. One 1999 sample, `alld99_e196_e1`, contains about 4.36 million events in XShort DST form; there are 2000 datasets with millions more. citeturn150907search2turn150907search0 There are also dedicated Bhabha simulations at the same energies, including barrel and forward samples. One barrel Bhabha sample at ~188 GeV is only about 88 MB, while some high-statistics forward samples run into several GB. citeturn252670search0turn252670search1\n\nSo from where you are now, I’d search/filter for:\n\n`DELPHI` → `181-210 GeV` → `e+e-`\n\nand distinguish **Collision** from **Simulated**.\n\nWhat I want first is not 70 GB of everything. CERN's DELPHI “Getting started” documentation points to actual DELPHI source and examples on CERN GitLab. The stack is also available in Docker, so in principle we can reconstruct the original analysis environment rather than reverse-engineering XShortDST ourselves. citeturn550381search0\n\nThe relevant source locations are linked from CERN's guide:\n\nurlDELPHI getting-started guidehttps://opendata.cern.ch/docs/delphi-getting-started\n\nand CERN says the source tree is under `gitlab.cern.ch/delphi`, with example repositories there; some modules still require CERN authentication, but the open examples should tell us how much we can do unauthenticated. citeturn550381search0\n\nThere's also a GitHub repository containing the source metadata/content behind CERN Open Data itself. The thing I’d watch is disk space, not RAM.\n\nFor your hardware, roughly:\n\n- Ubuntu under WSL: about 1–3 GB initially.\n- After installing compilers, libraries, CERN/DELPHI tools, expect more like 5–10 GB total.\n- A Docker-style image can easily add another several GB, sometimes 10+ GB depending on how fat the preserved environment is.\n- Idle RAM use is usually only a few hundred MB. While actually processing DELPHI data, I’d expect more like 1–3 GB for the sort of jobs we’re doing.\n- CPU: your i5-6300U is old and only 2 cores / 4 threads, but perfectly adequate for decoding and analyzing a 46 MB test sample. Large batch processing will simply be slow, not impossible.\n\nWith 12 GB RAM, I’m not worried. With a 168 GB SSD, I do not want us casually accumulating Docker layers, giant Monte Carlo sets, package caches, and duplicate CERN downloads.\n\nSo I’d actually change the plan slightly: install WSL Ubuntu, but avoid Docker Desktop unless we discover we specifically need it. Docker Desktop is substantially heavier than WSL itself and adds another virtualization/management layer you don’t need if we can run the DELPHI tools directly inside Linux.\n\nYour system is quite suitable for a lean setup:\n\nWindows\n→ WSL2\n→ Ubuntu\n→ DELPHI tools directly\n→ CERN files remain on your Windows drive and are accessed through `/mnt/c/...`\n\nThat means we do not need to duplicate the 46 MB file into Linux either.\n\nIf the preserved CERN environment turns out to be container-only, then we can install just the Docker engine inside WSL rather than the full Docker Desktop application. That would still be lighter.\n\nSo: yes, I’d install Ubuntu on this machine. I would not yet install Docker Desktop."

PDFs: should this be DOCX/PPTX instead?\n\nEven if the user asks for a PDF deliverable, the best workflow is often:\n\n- **Text-heavy, business-doc layout (headings, TOC, long tables, rich lists)** -> (PPTX) to author, then export to PDF.\n- **Programmatic generation** -> ReportLab (this skill) is fine.\n\nIf you find yourself hand-tuning line breaks or typography in ReportLab, you probably picked the wrong authoring format.\n\n---\n\n## Core loop (always)\n\n1) Render to images\n\n```bash\npython /home/oai/skills/pdfs/scripts/render_pdf.py input.pdf --out_dir /mnt/data/_renders/in --dpi 200\n```\n\n2) Inspect PNGs (tables/figures/layout are authoritative)\n\n3) Perform the edit/extract/create\n\n4) Re-render and compare\n\n```bash\npython             "Perfect. This is exactly the dataset we wanted.\n\nThe DELPHI submission gives us the electron angular distributions at 189–207 GeV in Tables 2–8, and the corresponding muon and tau distributions in Tables 11–18 and 21–28. fileciteturn6file0L708-L737 fileciteturn6file0L745-L768 fileciteturn6file0L775-L797\n\nThe electron tables alone already span roughly\n\n\\[\nQ^2=-t \\approx \\frac{s}{2}(1-\\cos\\theta)\n\\]\n\nfrom about \\(5\\times10^3\\) to \\(3.7\\times10^4\\ \\mathrm{GeV}^2\\) over the listed angular range. That corresponds to a naive spatial-resolution scale of order \\(10^{-18}\\) m. Precision fits can constrain smaller effective structure than that because they look for tiny systematic distortions of the angular distribution rather than literally “image” the electron.\n\nThe important thing I found in the DELPHI paper is that they already did essentially the kind of controlled deviation analysis we need. Their contact-interaction section writes the full differential cross section in terms of the Mandelstam variables and helicity amplitudes, then fits a deformation parameter \\(\\epsilon=1/\\Lambda^2\\) to the data. The fits included QED-radiation corrections and correlated systematic uncertainties. citeturn547441view2\n\nThat means we have two good routes now.\n\nThe conservative route is to use their published contact-interaction fits as an external scale constraint. For the electron channel they get characteristic scales of several to roughly 14 TeV depending on helicity structure. citeturn547441view2 That is not a literal radius, but it immediately tells us how little room there is for an extra short-distance interaction.\n\nThe more useful H(s)H route is to take the Tables 2–8 data and fit a deliberately geometric form-factor deformation, for example initially\n\n\\[\nF(Q^2)=1-\\frac{Q^2\\langle r^2\\rangle}{6}+\\cdots\n\\]\n\nor, better, several alternative transverse profiles rather than assuming a spherical charge distribution. Then we ask what effective scale the data allow.\n\nOne caution: the numbers you pasted are the measured cross sections, but not the full Standard Model baseline or covariance matrix. DELPHI says their interpretation used QED-corrected predictions and correlations, so to do a serious fit rather than a rough one we need those ingredients from the paper or associated analysis. citeturn547441view2\n\nSo the next thing I want is actually simpler than more raw data: download the full DELPHI paper, arXiv `hep-ex/0512012`, and if HEPData offers the entire submission as YAML/CSV, grab that too.\n\nOnce I have those, we can start extracting a real empirical constraint on the cross-section scale rather than just quoting somebody else's “electron radius.”"
